Why Davenport loses so many trees

Local measurements and geology — not national boilerplate.

99 / 99Iowa counties with confirmed emerald ash borer
86 mphderecho gust at Davenport Municipal Airport (Aug 2020)
2–4 yrsfrom EAB infestation to a dead ash tree
Silver maplethe most storm-downed tree in Davenport

Davenport's tree problem is a collision of two events. The emerald ash borer — confirmed in Davenport in June 2015 near Lincoln Avenue and Rockingham Road — has now been found in all 99 Iowa counties, and an infested ash dies in roughly two to four years. Ash made up a large share of the city's street and yard plantings, and the city removes right-of-way ash trees rather than treating them unless the adjacent resident pays for treatment. Layered on top: the August 10, 2020 derecho drove an 86 mph gust through Davenport Municipal Airport and left the city arborist describing local tree losses as “uncountable.” The result is a standing backlog of dead ash and storm-weakened maples that keeps removal crews working year-round.

Sources: Iowa Dept. of Agriculture & Land Stewardship (EAB in all 99 counties); Quad-City Times (Davenport EAB confirmation); NWS/KWQC derecho wind surveys; City of Davenport Public Works

What a professional removal actually involves

Most Davenport removals are not one clean cut at the base. In a yard with structures, fences, or lines nearby, the tree comes down as a sectional dismantle: a climber or bucket operator takes the canopy apart limb by limb, rigging each piece on ropes so nothing free-falls, then blocks the trunk down in rounds. Open-felling in one piece happens only where there is genuinely room to lay the whole tree down — rarer in town than people expect.

Davenport's older neighborhoods are dominated by big, fast-grown silver maples — soft-wooded, prone to hollow spots, and the most frequently downed species in the 2020 derecho — plus a heavy legacy ash population now dying on the borer's schedule. A dead tree raises the stakes: dry, brittle wood does not bend or hold rigging the way live wood does, which is why a standing dead ash is more dangerous — and often more expensive — to remove than a live tree of the same size. The longer it stands, the worse both problems get.

  • Sectional dismantles with rigging — nothing free-falls near structures
  • Dead and dying ash removals, including brittle EAB-killed trees
  • Wood hauled, brush chipped, and the yard raked before the crew leaves
  • Proof of insurance available on request — ask, every time, for anyone you hire

Davenport Tree Removal — FAQ

How much does tree removal cost in Davenport?
Most Davenport removals fall between $450 and $1,200 for a mid-size tree (30–60 ft); small ornamentals run $350–$435, and large 60–80 ft shade trees start around $1,500 and climb with access difficulty. Access, height, condition, and what is under the tree move the price more than the species does. Get the quote in writing and confirm whether stump grinding is included — usually it is not.
Do I need a permit to remove a tree in Davenport?
On your own property, Davenport does not generally require a permit to remove your own tree. The line that matters is the right-of-way: trees on city property or the strip along the street cannot be removed, cut, or trimmed without authorization from the city arborist, per the City of Davenport Tree Ordinance. If in doubt about where the right-of-way ends, Public Works (563.326.7923) can tell you before anyone cuts.
How fast can a tree in contact with my house be handled?
A tree actually on or against a structure is emergency work and is typically handled same-day or next-day. If a power line is involved, call the utility first — tree crews cannot legally touch a tree that is energized through a service line.
Should I remove my ash tree even if it looks fine?
In Scott County, an untreated ash is on borrowed time — emerald ash borer kills an infested tree in roughly two to four years, and the damage is well underway before the canopy visibly thins. Removing a still-sound ash is routine work; removing a brittle dead one is hazard work at hazard prices. If you want to keep the tree, ongoing insecticide treatment is the only path.
